title: parameterized paths

milestone.title: MVP
milestone.description:
- obvious functionality such as reading / writing headers 
- sufficient unit test coverage
- documentation  
- metadata in package.json

body:
Sometimes a parameter appears in the middle of a path, e.g.:

```
/users/{user_id}/profile
/users/{user_id}/friends
/users/{user_id}/preferences
```

The filesystem based routing scheme doesn't currently accommodate this use case well. Ideally we would model the above like so:

```
- users
   - user_id
       - friends.js
       - preferences.js
       - profile.js
 ```
  

But that will only match these URLs

```
/users/user_id/friends
/users/user_id/preferences
/users/user_id/profile
 ```

Whereas we want it to match URLs that look like this:

```
/users/12345/friends
/users/12345/preferences
/users/12345/profile

/users/86753/friends
/users/86753/preferences
/users/86753/profile

/users/99999/friends
/users/99999/preferences
/users/99999/profile
```

We need a way to identify that the `user_id` directory is a wildcard, not meant to be matched literally. Where would be the right place to encode that information? How about in `user.js`?

```
- users
   - user_id
       - friends.js
       - preferences.js
       - profile.js
- users.js <--- here
 ```

```js
// users.js 
const USER_ID_REGEX = /^\d{3,10}$/;

export function wildcard(key) {
   if(USER_ID_REGEX.test(key) { 
       return 'user_id';
   } 
   return key;
}
```

When parsing the URL `/users/99999/profile`, Counterfact will look at users.js and find that it has a wildcard function. Since "99999" is a valid user ID, it will next look for `./users/user_id.js` and `./users/user_id/profile.js` instead of `./users/99999.js` and `./users/99999/profile.js`

Profile.js will then look something like this:
```js
//profile.js

export function GET({path, store}) {
   return {
      body: `User profile for ${path.user_id}: ${store.users[path.user_id].profile}`
   }
}

export function PUT({path, store, body}) {
    store.users[path.user_id].profile = body;
   return {
      body: `ok`
   }
}

```

title: dynamic routes
Point Counterfact to a JS file rather than a directory

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

body:
Currently the base path is expected to be a directory.

```
my-app
   /routes <-- here
      /articles
         /[articleId].js
      /categories.js
```

However, the base path could be a file. 
```
my-app
   /routes
      /articles
         /[articleId].js
      /categories.js
   /routes.js <-- here
```

And that makes a lot of sense, because that top level file could implement default handlers for each of the request methods.

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

title: Install husky and run eslint after commits
body:
Normally ESLint is run as a pre-commit hook.

But having a commit blocked because of lint errors can be annoying sometimes.
Sometimes I'm okay with things being broken temporarily; CI will run ESLint
and prevent the offending code from landing on main.

But then there's a new problem. Code is committed and pushed, and then CI
fails because of a silly lint error. I'm giving the post-commit hook at try
so I can find out immediately if the code I just pushed will break CI.

Let's see how this goes...

body:

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

title: proof of concept supporting TypeScript
body:
We can convert our route files to TypeScript, run the app through ts-node, and it "just works". 

In the example, we're importing types from a "special" file called `#types`. The idea is this file can be generated from from an OpenAPI spec. 

That mostly resolves #43 but I want to dot some `i`s and cross some `t`s  before closing that issue.

title: Add a tools object that will be provided to the request
body:
It provides some useful functionality:


- `tools.oneOf(array)` returns a random item from an array (used for selecting a random example from a an OpenAPI schema)
- `tools.accepts(contentType)` identifies whether the request accepts a particular content type

title: Generator: fill in missing unit tests

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body:
The word "path" in this codebase can mean a few different things:

- a file path
- a path in the tree structure of a JSON / YAML file
- node's built-in path module

To ease the confusion, everywhere we import path, the code should be:

```js
import nodePath from "node:path";
```

Avoid these patterns:

```js
import path from "node:path";
import { join } from "node:path"; 
```

title: Build ASTs instead of printing code directly

labels.name: archive
labels.description: Mostly Patrick brainstorming in the early days

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

body:
The TypeScript generator might be easier to read, maintain, and test if it built up ASTs rather cobbling strings together with template literals. 

A couple of libraries we could use:

- https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/wiki/Using-the-Compiler-API
- https://github.com/dsherret/ts-morph

It can be done one `Coder` at a time and we may decided part of the way through that it's not a good idea. The first step is to implement the base `Coder#write()` method like so:

```
write(script) {
    return printer.print(this.buildAst(script)); 
}
```

Then within each subclass create a `buildAst()` method and delete the `write()` method.

https://mswjs.io/docs/comparison

Now it's also taken on generating TypeScript code from OpenAPI. Because I couldn't find anything that generates TypeScript code that I found to be sufficiently readable and easy to relate back to the source.

title: init command to create create a complete package

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body:
```sh
npx counterfact init ./path/to/openapi.yaml ./path/to/package
```

Counterfact should create a package that looks similar to the current [demo-ts](https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/tree/main/demo-ts) directory. So that in the end these four commands will result in a running server. 

```sh
npx counterfact init ./path/to/openapi.yaml ./path/to/package
cd ./path/to/package
npm install
npm start
```

In time, we'll add prompts to make sure the user really wants to create a whole new package, whether they want it to use Koa or Express, whether it should run npm install, initialize a git repo, commit the code, generate unit tests, etc. For version 1.0, all that matters is that we make getting started and kicking the tires redonkulously easy.

Currently the `generate` command expects the OpenAPI spec to be a file path. It should also work if passed an HTTP or HTTPS URL.

### Add the Open API document to $

body:
Given the following schema:

```yaml
type: object
  additionalProperties:
    type: integer
```

SchemaTypeCoder should yield the following type:

```ts
{
    [k: string]: number
}
```

However, given the following schema.

```yaml
type: object
  properties:
    name: firstName
    type: string 
  additionalProperties:
    type: integer
```

All properties _except_ name should be numbers. [TypeScript currently has no way to represent an object with some properties that have one type and all other properties of another type.](
https://github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/17867) The best we can do is this:

```ts
{
    name?: string
    [k: string]: unknown
}
```

It also needs to handle the case where `additionalProperties` is `true` or `false`.

Now that I've written it out I realize it boils down to something like this.

```js

if (hasAdditionalProperties) {
    if(hasProperties) {
       append('[k: string]: unknown')
    } else {
       append(`[k: string]: ${additionalProperties.type}`)
    } 
}
```

I don't really care about this case at this point, but if ALL of the properties happen to have the same type as `additionalProperties`, then we can resolve the type instead of putting `unknown` in.

title: Version Packages
body:
This PR was opened by the [Changesets release](https://github.com/changesets/action) GitHub action. When you're ready to do a release, you can merge this and the packages will be published to npm automatically. If you're not ready to do a release yet, that's fine, whenever you add more changesets to main, this PR will be updated.


# Releases
## counterfact@0.7.0

### Minor Changes

-   4f3c7c9: define a ResponseBuilder type -- to be refined later with one or more generic arguments
-   5f3ee3f: response builder fluent API which is going to make intellisense with TypeScript awesome
-   6221e7d: `counterfact start` command to start a server
-   a3dfb48: `npm counterfact init <openapi-file> <destination>` command to build a new package with a Counterfact server
-   9f91d57: adds a 'go' command that generates code and starts the server in one step
-   25dcd45: ability to respond with multiple content types, return the best match for the request's accept header
-   c84a4f4: Counterfact is now able to read an OpenAPI document and use it to generate a random response.
-   c0cb938: a function can now return "hello world" as shorthand for `{status: 200, contentType: "text/plain", body: "hello world"}`

### Patch Changes

-   69b4598: replaced EventEmitter with EventTarget
-   a07c2b2: fix a crash when regenerating code
-   85c3349: fixed an issue where hot reload did not work in some cases
-   1551cbb: handle additionalProperties when converting a JSON Schema to TypeScript

title: Interact with the context via the the browser's dev tools (remote procedure call)

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

body:
Similar to #86 

For testing purpose, I would like to make access runtime access to the `context` object at the heart of a server as convenient as possible. Why not expose it through the browser's dev tools?

Not necessarily _direct_ access. What I'm thinking is we create a proxy context object that runs in the browser, with method signatures matching the context object on the server. When you call `context.reticulate('splines')` on the browser object, it sends the method name and arguments to the server via a web socket. Counterfact then intercepts that request on the server side and calls `context.reticulate('splines')` on the server object. The return value is then `JSON.stringify()`ed and returned to the client. 

Two consequences of this remote procedure call (RPC) approach:

1. It only works on methods that take JSON-serializable objects as arguments and return JSON-serializable values. Maybe we can use TypeScript to enforce that _all_ context methods follow this convention. That feels like a good idea anyway, as it will encourage people to move business logic into the `Context` class instead of the `/paths/**/*.ts` files. 

3. Every method on the client-side context object is asynchronous. If we care about the return value we need to use `await x = context.reticulate('splines')` even if the `reticulate()` method is synchronous on the server side.

title: Overwrite individual functions in paths/**/*.ts files if they haven't changed

labels.name: archive
labels.description: Mostly Patrick brainstorming in the early days

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

body:
Let's say Counterfact generates a GET function and a POST function in /paths/pets.ts

We change the GET function but leave the POST function alone. After making a change to the OpenAPI document, we want to recreate all generated code without overwriting manually edited code. 

For that reason, Counterfact currently will not touch any file under paths if a file already exists. 

Instead of ignoring the file completely, ideally it would leave the GET function alone and recreate the POST function. 

To make this work, we can create an index file which keeps track of all generated functions and hashes of their ASTs. If a given function already exists, but it's hash has not changed, we know it's safe to recreate that function. Otherwise leave it alone. 

Theoretically this same logic could be applied to other files, allowing users to make changes to the generated types if they so desire. I don't think we should encourage that behavior but it could be an option that's off by default.

title: npx counterfact start

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

Add a parameter to the verb functions called `response`. The API looks like this. ```js response[statusCode] .header("a-string-header", "value") .header("a-number-header", 100) .match("content/type", "body") .match("another/type", "body") .json({ isJson: true }) // shortcut for .match("application/json", ...) .text("text") // shortcut for .match("text/plain", ...) .html("

html

"); // shortcut for .match("text/html", ...) ``` The return value is a response object. ```js const response = { statusCode: statusCode, headers: { ... }, contentType: { "text/plain": "text body", "application/json": {json: "body"} } } ``` If someone else picks this up I'll add more detail. But I'll probably get to it myself today.

body:
Handle multiple response types in the same return statement (without if (accepts(...)))). 

Currently the return type of a verb function looks like this:

```ts
type returnType = {
   status: HttpStatusCode,
   contentType: `${string}/${string}",
   headers: Record<string, string | number>,
   body: unknown
}
```

We need a way to handle a scenario where the API can return two or more different content types depending on what the client accepts.

```ts
type returnType = {
   status: HttpStatusCode,
   headers: Record<string, string | number>,
  content: { 
          media: `${string}/${string}",
          body: unknown
      }[],
}
```

In this case, the server will loop through each item in the content array and return the content-type + body of the first one that matches. If there are no matches it will return a 415 status code (or whatever code is most appropriate, need to double check that).

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body:
Building on #133

`response[statusCode].random()` returns a valid, randomly generated response, based on the schema provided by an OpenAPI document. 

For now, `response[statusCode].header('x-header', 'whatever').json('whatever').random()` ignores the header and content that were provided and provides a completely random value. In the future we'll want to keep whatever was provided and only randomize the parts that were not specified. In the future we'll want to keep whatever is provided and only randomize the remainder. 

In order for `random()` to work we need to provide Counterfact the OpenAPI document at runtime. It can be passed into the constructor. If Counterfact doesn't have an OpenAPI spec, return a 500 error with an explanation. 

This issue does not include type checking. That's covered in #136

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
```

title: hot reload doesn't work in some cases
body:
1. run `yarn start demo` 
2. open http://localhost:3100/hello/world
3. make a change to `./demo/hello/{name}.js` 
4. reload  http://localhost:3100/hello/world

The change made in step 3 should be reflected. 

It's not because of this line in module-loader.js

```js
        const url = `/${nodePath.join(parts.dir, parts.name)}`;
```

The path already starts with a `/` so the URL ends up starting with `//`. 

I think it depends on whether `parts.dir` ends with a `/`. 

Anyway, I think it's an easy fix. Just wrap the whole thing in `nodePath.normalize()`.

body:
As of #135, examples in a _schema_ are used to generate random values. It does not yet use [examples at the content level](https://swagger.io/docs/specification/adding-examples/).


```yaml
responses:
  '200':
    description: A user object.
    content:
      application/json:
        schema:
          $ref: '#/components/schemas/User'   # Reference to an object
        examples:
          Jessica:
            value:
              id: 10
              name: Jessica Smith
          Ron:
            value:
              id: 20
              name: Ron Stewart
```

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

body:
The following command should start a server from the base directory (defaulting to the current working directory).

```sh
npx counterfact [baseDir] [pathToOpenApi]
```

If an OpenAPI file is given, it will first generate TypeScript code from that file. It should also watch the file and regenerate the types whenever it changes. Thus combining the functionality of the current `start` and `generate` commands.

The `init` command will go away. It's not useful enough to warrant the added complexity.

title: Change `requirement.select()` so we don't have to replace "/" with "~1"

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body:
Code like this

```ts
      const property = this.requirement.select(`properties/${name}`);
```

Can be rewritten as

```ts
      const property = this.requirement.select("properties").select(name);
```

If we change `select()` so that it only takes one step, then we escape the "/" in a value. So code like this:

```ts
        const schema = responses
          .select(type.responseCode)
          .select("content")
          ?.select(type.contentType.replace("/", "~1"))
          ?.select("schema");
```

Becomes this:

```ts
        const schema = responses
          .select(type.responseCode)
          .select("content")
          ?.select(type.contentType)
          ?.select("schema");
```

title: The OpenAPI document is not getting loaded at runtime

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body: Since #157 the OpenAPI document path is not passed into not passed into the `counterfact()` function. So we can't use `response[statusCode].random()`.

### Add the Open API document to $

body:
`response[statusCode].random()` uses JSONSchemaFaker to generate a random response. As long as the schema for the response is inline it works. It needs to be extended to work when the response is at a `$ref`. We need to either resolve all the references before calling JSONSchemaFaker or use it's `resolve()` method. 

Maybe use https://github.com/APIDevTools/json-schema-ref-parser to dereference the OpenAPI document at the time it's loaded. We need to trace the references at build time so we can generate TypeScript with a file structure that matches the structure at the document. At runtime, when we're using the document to generate random data, we don't care about where the data came from. We just want a simple JSON object.

title: Finalize the CLI for version 1.0

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body:
Here's what I'm thinking:

```sh
npx counterfact <open-api-location> [target] [--serve <port>] [--swagger] [--open]
```

## Options

### open-api-location

An http(s) URL or file path pointing to an OpenAPI v3 document.

### target

The location where generated files will go. The default is the current working directory.

### --serve \<port\>

Start a web server at the given port (default 3000).

### --swagger

Attach swagger-ui to the server (implies _--server_).

### --open

Open a browser to swagger-ui (implies _--swagger_). 


## Example

```sh
npx counterfact https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.json --open 
```

The above command will read the pet store example, generate TypeScript code, start the server, and open a browser to Swagger UI. This is the "hello world" demo I've been working toward.

title: Landing page

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body:
When the CLI is run with the `--open` flag, it now opens to Swagger UI.

That's probably find for day-to-day use, but a little disorienting if this is the first time you've seen Counterfact. Instead I would like to open to a documentation page that covers:

- What is Counterfact
- What is Open API
- Big button / link to open Swagger UI
- How paths map to TypeScript files
- Building a response
- Hot reloading
- Request parameters: `path`, `query`, `headers` and `body`
- Working with state (`context` and `$context.ts`)
- Planned features

title: Non-alphanumeric characters in the component name break the code generator.
body:
To reproduce:

```sh
yarn counterfact https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stripe/openapi/master/openapi/spec3.yaml stripe
```

It results in an error. 

```
SyntaxError: ',' expected. (4:19)
  2 | import type { HttpStatusCode } from "counterfact";
  3 | import Context from "./../../../paths/v1/apps/$context.js";
> 4 | import type { apps.secret } from "./../../../components/apps.secret.js";
    |                   ^
```

There's a component (under schemas) named `apps.secret`. That's not a valid variable name so we need to transform it to something like `apps_secret`.

title: $context.js files aren't generated for in-between directories
body: Say an OpenAPI spec defines `/foo/bar/baz` and no other paths. When Counterfact generates`/foo/bar/$context.ts` it creates `/foo/bar/baz.ts` which references `/foo/$context.ts`. But since it's not generating any `/foo/*.ts` files it won't create the `/foo/$context.ts` file.

title: When adding a server URL, add the full URL
body: Counterfact includes Swagger-UI. I loads the OpenAPI document through a proxy which puts itself at the top of the `servers` list in the OpenAPI document. Currently the URL it adds is just "/".  If the OpenAPI document has an entry for host, it will try to load `/` on the host instead of the localhost. To fix that, we need to change the "/" to "http://localhost:${port}/".

- start with VSCode, a file of snippets to cut and paste

title: Proxy

labels.name: archive
labels.description: Mostly Patrick brainstorming in the early days

milestone.title: Future
milestone.description: Future enhancements that are not (yet) tied to any upcoming release

body:
Support proxying to another server instead of using mocks. In addition to supporting the ability to proxy to another server, there are five different interfaces through which we may turn the proxy on or off.

## CLI
- [x] `--proxy-url [url]` to set the proxy URL

## Code
- [ ] `return $.proxy();` to use the proxy for an operation -- if no proxy is set return 502
- [x] `return $.proxy('https://example.com/specific-url');` to use the proxy via a specific URL

## REPL
- [x] `.proxy` to toggle the proxy globally
- [x] #440


## REST
To support the GUI

- [ ] `POST /counterfact/proxy/{url}` with the URL in the body to set the proxy URL
- [ ] `POST /counterfact/proxy` with `true` or `false` in the body to enable disable the proxy globally
- [ ] `GET /counterfact/proxy` to list individual operations and whether they're proxid 
- [ ] `POST /counterfact/proxy/operations` with an `{ path, method, isEnabled }[]` to toggle the proxy for individual URLs



## GUI
- [ ] a toggle to turn the proxy on and off
- [ ] an input to set the proxy URL
- [ ] individual toggles for each route

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

title: saturday refactoring
body:
- change flatMap signature so the callback is (value, key) => result
- change requirement.map signature so the callback is (value, key) => result
- now that map() is refactored, flatMap() can got back to delegating to it
- change requirement.forEach signature so the callback is (value, key) => result
- refactor responseTypeCoder.normalizeStatusCode()
- simplify ResponseTypeCoder.buildContentObjectType
- simplify responseTypeCoder.buildHeaders
- rename variable for consistency with buildHeaders
- new printObjectFromEntries() function
- use printObjectFromEntries() in responseTypeCoder.buildHeaders()
- refactor ResponseTypeCoder so few arguments are passed around
- teasing apart ASTs and printers a little bit at a time


Some things I'm thinking about next:

1. There's an opportunity now for `requirement.get(key)` to return a NullRequirement instead of `undefined`.
2. Might want to `.keys()`, `.values()`, and `.entries()` to `Requirement`. 
3. I don't like `requirement.data`. I think it should be `requirement.value`. 
4. Still lots of low-hanging fruit in the `typescript-generator` 
5. Need to add more unit tests and rely less on snapshots

title: OpenAPI 2 support
body:
Add support for OpenAPI 2. This is hacky. More unit tests are needed. I should look at the actual spec version rather than duck type. 

Maybe create subclasses of each Coder for OpenAPI 2. That implies a factory for creating coders instead of calling their constructors directly. That may be a better design in the long run, but I don't think I want to deal with that right now. 

- add a shortcut for generating (testing) pet store v2
- support for OAS2 parameter, where there is not a separate schema object
- generate a default response for an OAS2 operation
- refactoring caused whitespace changes in the snapshot
- generate the response type for OAS2
- move the code to copy response-builder-factory.ts into generate()
- move copying response-builder-factory.ts into repository.js
- refactoring changed whitespace in the snapshot
- support OpenAPI2 when building the response object
- don't start the server when testing via yarn go:petstore
- support the request body in OpenAPI 2
- consistently set request properties to 'never' when they should not be there

title: Harden support for Open API 2

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

body: I hacked in OpenAPI 2 support (#276) so I could get something out there. There's no testing around it, and it uses a sort of duck typing rather than looking at the version number of the spec.

title: use OpenAPI to convert strings in path/query/header to numbers
body:
When a path is defined as `/pet/{id}` and OpenAPI says `id` is a number, it's treated as a number in TypeScript. In JavaScript at runtime, it needs to be converted from a number to a string. The same goes for parameters in the query string or headers.

I'm not sure what to do about booleans as there's no standard conversion from string to boolean (e.g. `"yes"` becomes `true` and `"no"` becomes `false`). I don't think OpenAPI has a solution for that. 

More complex types, such as `Array` and `Object`, are not currently supported by Counterfact.

To do: 

- [x] refactor so that the object passed into registry.endpoint() is more to the point
- [ ] make sure OpenAPI/Swagger 2.0 is supported
- [ ] add some lower-level unit tests

title: Correct main and exports properties
body:
When I try to import from `'./src/server/counterfact.js'` I get this error:

`Package subpath './src/server/counterfact.js' is not defined by "exports" ` in the `package.json`. Is this change the right one to fix it? I don't think I have this right because when I change this directly in `node_modules` it still gives the same error.

Related to this question, but not present in the PR is the `types` property which is set to `./src/counterfact.d.ts` in the `package.json` file but doesn't actually exist in the project. Does that need to be addressed?

title: Export the swaggerUi middleware
body: This exports the swaggerUi function so that if an implementing server wants to add the swagger middleware alongside the koaMiddleware that exposes the API they can do so.

title: Swagger UI posts to the "host" from the spec instead of localhost
body: I have Counterfact spun up and it has processed our API, successfully rendering the Swagger UI. When I try to execute any of our endpoints instead of posting them against the counterfact server on localhost, it posts them against the URL specific in the `"hosts"` key in the openapi file.

Brainstorming. Thinking about putting this in the README. 

| |Counterfact|Your Production Back End|
|-|-|-|
|To front end code it's...|a fully functional REST API|a fully functional REST API|

|Running locally requires|node| probably a lot more than that |
|See code changes|when you hit save | after compile + restart / deploy |
|Change behavior without losing server-side state| yes (hot reload) | wait, what?|
|Play with the state in a REPL | yes | not likely |
|Maintainable by front end devs | yes | maybe?|
|Reproducing weird stuff that happened in prod | easy | hard / impossible |
|API response time|negligible|varies|
|Maintaining test accounts is | optional | required |
|Integrates with UI tests (Jest, Playwright, etc.)| [coming soon] |no|
|Seed with test data / scenarios| [coming soon] | much slower if possible at all |
|Optimized for | developers | end users |
|Developer experience | 😁 | 😣 |


<sup>1</sup> a change big enough to call out in release notes

title: Add the Open API document to $

labels.name: archive
labels.description: Mostly Patrick brainstorming in the early days

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```

title: Missing type definition for path parameters
body: Given the path `/foo/{id}`, there should be a property called `$.path.id`. It's there at runtime but missing in the TypeScript definition.

title: Add a comment to the top of generated files

milestone.title: Version 1.0
milestone.description:
This project will reach 1.0 when mutation test coverage is > 90% and:

The following command

```sh
npx counterfact init ./my-petstore https://petstore3.swagger.io/api/v3/openapi.yaml
```

creates or augments an npm package, and after changing to the directory

```sh
cd my-petstore
```

the following command

```sh
yarn start

```

opens a browser with Swagger-UI pointing to a server that implements the pet store API.

Not a mock server that returns canned or randomly generated responses, a real implementation, written in TypeScript.

Or at least, the potential for a real implementation. Out of the box, it will return example or random responses. But the code is easy to edit so, e.g., we can change PUT /pet to store a Pet in memory / a database / a microservice / etc., and GET /pet to retrieve that same Pet.

We can see the effects of the code changes without restarting the server.

And then after running

```sh
npm run counterfact generate /path/to/copy/of/petstore/with/some/changes.yaml
```

it regenerates the code except for the files that we changed. Of the files we changed, the IDE (via TypeScript and ESLint) tells us if the code needs to be modified to conform to the updated spec.

Again, without restarting the server.


---- 

Update 2913-09-06

All of the above is done except 90% test coverage (which is close). In fact, it works a lot better than what I wrote above. There are a few little tweaks I would like to add before stamping 1.0 and spreading the word. 


## GUI (web page)

Add a field to enter the proxy address, and a checkbox / toggle to turn it on and off globally.

Put the list of paths in a table and add columns for:

- proxy (checkbox or toggle)
- methods (one or multiple columns with icons representing the standard HTTP methods)
  - could link directly to the implementations for each method in the IDE

Use a websocket to keep the above information current.

Put a REPL in the GUI.

## Config file

`.counterfact.yaml` can have the path to the OpenAPI spec, the proxy URL, whether the proxy is on (globally), and whether the proxy is on for individual paths

An "extends" field so we can have a base config which is committed to the repo and a local config which is in `.gitignore`

## Code generation

Use the OpenAPI spec to generate JSDocs.

Move `paths-js` to `.cache` to make it clear these files aren't meant to be edited.

Import models that will likely be useful. (https://github.com/pmcelhaney/counterfact/issues/529)

## Watch the OpenAPI file

If the OpenAPI file is local, watch it for changes and regenerate code.

## TypeScript

While Counterfact generates TypeScript, Counterfact itself was originally written in JavaScript. The server code is now in TypeScript. Now just need to update the typescript-generator code.

## REPL

Finalize the API for `.proxy`: `.proxy [on|off [path]]`, `.proxy set url`

## Server

### Add the Open API document to $

The particular use case I have in mind is being able to pass a schema to json-schema-faker, so that we can exercise fine-grained control over what is generated.

```ts
export const GET: HTTP_GET = ($) => {
  const randomPet = jsf.generate($.openapi.components.schemas.Pet.schema);
  return $.response[200].json(randomPet);
};
```
